extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students studying U.S. patent infringement defences
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for defenses available to a defendant in an action for patent infringement under the U.S. patent statutes (c.1836), including substantive grounds (novelty, utility, enablement, subject-matter) and procedural pleading/notice requirements for special matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of infringement / non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show, under the general issue, without notice, that he never did the act complained of, that is, that he has not infringed the patent, or that he was acting under a license or purchase from the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative factual denial of the alleged infringing act is a complete defense to the action; evidence of a license or a purchase from the plaintiff defeats the claim of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff status and title defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that the plaintiff is an alien, not entitled to a patent; or that the plaintiff has not a good title as assignee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenses attacking the plaintiff's entitlement or title (e.g., lack of nationality entitlement, defective assignment/title) can be asserted to defeat recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent not duly issued (formal defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that his patent was not duly issued according to law, in respect of the signatures of the public officers, or of the public seal, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of formal irregularities in issuance (signatures, seal, other ministerial prerequisites) may be offered as a defense to the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Admitting its novelty, the defendant may show that the invention is not an 'art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter,' in the sense of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant can concede novelty but argue that the claimed subject-matter falls outside statutory categories of patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of novelty must be specified (statutory special defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defence that the subject is not patentable on the ground of want of novelty falls under the statute, and must be specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/anticipation is a statutory special matter: when relied upon, it must be pleaded or noticed according to the statute (see notice requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of utility (worthlessness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show, under the general issue, without notice, that the invention, though new, fails in point of utility, and is worthless and frivolous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Want of utility is not enumerated in the §15 list but is nevertheless a clear bar to the action and may be raised without the special notice required for some other defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification absence or ambiguity (uncertainty / indefiniteness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant may show that there is no specification, or that the specification is so ambiguous and unintelligible that the court cannot determine from it what the invention is intended to be patented; in such case the patent is void for ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a distinct issue from statutory special matters and can be put in issue by a plea of not guilty; the specification must enable the court and the public to ascertain what is claimed with reasonable certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment or addition in specification made to deceive the public
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification contains some concealment or addition made for the purpose of deceiving the public, and it is intended to show this under the general issue, notice must be given (special defence under the statute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of fraudulent concealment or addition in the specification are treated as special matters under the statute and require the statutory notice; they are the grounds on which a court may be asked to declare a patent void for fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must be full, clear, and exact; enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires that the inventor deliver a written description of his invention 'in such full, clear, and exact terms, as to distinguish the same from all other things before known, and ... to enable any person skilled in the art or science ... to make, compound, and use the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement: specification must explain the principle and several modes of application; it need not teach persons of every capacity but must enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to construct and use the invention. Failure to meet these pre-requisites is a defense to infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish new from old; claims must appear with reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must describe, in full and exact terms, what his invention consists of and distinguish what is new from what is old; what is claimed as new must appear with reasonable certainty on the face of the patent, either expressly or by necessary implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification mixes up old and new, or leaves the scope of what is claimed to minute references and conjecture, the patent is void; courts look for reasonable certainty in the claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent intent required to annul patent under §6/§15
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify a judgment declaring a patent void on account of concealment or addition in the specification, the defect or concealment must appear to have been made for the purpose of deceiving the public; evidence of fraudulent intent is requisite only for the particular purpose of having the patent declared void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a distinction between defenses that defeat recovery in a single suit and those that will lead to a judgment declaring the patent void; the latter generally require proof of intent to deceive as prescribed by the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading and notice rules for special matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute provides that the defendant may, under the general issue, give the statute itself in evidence and certain special matters, of which he shall have given notice in writing to the plaintiff or his attorney thirty days before trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special defenses enumerated by statute must be either specially pleaded (setting forth defects and charging intent) or presented under the general issue accompanied by the statutory written notice; strict compliance with notice rules is required when the statute mandates it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior knowledge / prior use / anticipation defence and required specificity in notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The special defence that 'the patentee was not the original and first inventor or discoverer' or that the invention had been described in a public work anterior to the patentee's discovery requires the defendant to show the invention had been known, used, or described earlier; the defendant must state in his notice the names and places of residence of those he intends to prove to have possessed prior knowledge and where the same had been used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must strictly describe whether the whole or part of the invention is charged with want of novelty and identify the prior public work(s); this provision must be strictly complied with and has no time limitation for when the defence may be set up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory provisos limiting prior-use attack and equitable relief on overbroad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisos: (1) if it satisfactorily appears that the patentee, at the time of application, believed himself to be the first inventor, the patent shall not be held void because of prior foreign use, unless the subject had been previously patented or described in printed publication; (2) if plaintiff fails because his specification/claim embraces more than he invented, but the defendant has used any part truly specified and claimed as new, the court may adjudge costs as just and equitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisos moderate the harshness of a strict prior-use/anticipation rule and permit equitable allocation of costs when part of a claim is genuinely new and infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of skill for enablement inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is judged by whether a person skilled in the art or science, of which the invention is a branch, or with which it is most nearly connected, would be enabled to construct the invention from the specification; it is not necessary to teach at the level of every person's capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply a 'person of ordinary skill in the art' standard (examples in text: 'pump-maker of ordinary skill'); overly obscure or materially defective specifications that prevent such a skilled person from practice can bar recovery.
